desc:
A directed graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry edges[i] = [a, b] is a one-way edge from a to b. A self-loop [a, a] is allowed.

Starting at node s, you must follow at least one edge, always in its direction. Return true if you can arrive back at s, which means that s lies on a directed cycle. Return false otherwise.

n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[2,3]], s = 1  ->  true   (1 -> 2 -> 0 -> 1)
n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[2,3]], s = 3  ->  false  (node 3 has no outgoing edge)
n = 2, edges = [[0,0]],                  s = 0  ->  true   (the self-loop)
n = 2, edges = [[0,1]],                  s = 0  ->  false
constraints: No directed edge appears twice; self-loops are allowed
hints: You are not asking whether a path from s to t exists for some other t; the target is s itself, and the walk has to use at least one edge.
Start the search from the nodes that s points to, not from s with 'already visited'.
Mark all out-neighbours of s as visited and push them. Run a DFS or BFS along directed edges. As soon as s itself is reached, answer true; if the search ends first, answer false.
editorial: The node s is on a directed cycle exactly when there is a walk of one or more edges from s back to s. A search that begins at s and marks s visited immediately would never notice such a walk, so the trick is to seed the search with the out-neighbours of s only.

Mark every out-neighbour of s as visited and put it on a stack. Pop a node; if it is s, a walk of at least one edge has come back and the answer is true. Otherwise visit its unvisited out-neighbours. A self-loop is handled automatically, because s is then among its own out-neighbours. If the stack empties, s cannot be reached again and the answer is false.

Each node is pushed at most once and each edge is looked at once, so the time is O(n + m). Running a full cycle-detection for the whole graph would answer more than is asked; the question is about one node.
